title: Generic Relationships and Constraints
learning_outcomes: Explain relating input and output types in the context of generic relationships and constraints.
Apply the lesson concept in a small TypeScript example and describe what the compiler can check.
Identify one limitation or failure case and choose an appropriate runtime check or test when needed.

content.intro: Learn generic relationships and constraints through a compact mental model, syllabus-aligned subtopics, a worked example and a practical task. The goal is not to memorize syntax but to know what the type contract guarantees and what evidence is still needed.
content.why_it_matters: Model the narrowest honest type contract. Prefer inference where it is clear, use unknown at untrusted boundaries, and use control-flow checks before performing operations that depend on a value’s shape.

content_blocks.title: Mental model
content_blocks.text: **Generic Relationships and Constraints.** This lesson belongs to **Generics and Reusable Components**. Start by identifying the problem that generic relationships and constraints solves. In TypeScript, separate three questions: what values your program intends to accept, what the compiler can prove from the code, and what must still be checked while the program runs. The last category matters whenever data comes from a user, file, API, storage layer, or an untyped JavaScript dependency.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics and how to use them

items.title: Relating input and output types
items.text: For relating input and output types, treat incoming values as untrusted until runtime checks establish the required shape. A TypeScript annotation does not validate network, file, database, storage, or user-provided data by itself.

items.title: Generic callbacks
items.text: For generic callbacks, write down the input contract and the result contract. Let TypeScript infer obvious local types, and add annotations where they clarify a public API, callback, or boundary.

items.title: Constraints that preserve useful information
items.text: For constraints that preserve useful information, connect the concept to a small concrete example, state the assumption it relies on, and verify the result with a compiler diagnostic or a runtime test as appropriate.

content_blocks.title: Example: Generic Relationships and Constraints
content_blocks.expected_output: Runtime output: TYPESCRIPT. The generic preserves the precise string type.

content_blocks.title: Compile-time versus runtime
content_blocks.text: Type annotations and most type declarations are erased when TypeScript emits JavaScript. They do not validate external JSON, authorize a user, sanitize HTML, or prevent runtime failures by themselves. Validate trust-boundary inputs and test the behavior.

content.task: Create a small TypeScript example for “Generic Relationships and Constraints”. Demonstrate relating input and output types, explain your assumption, and include one check that shows the expected behavior. Do not treat a type annotation as runtime validation for external input.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one syllabus subtopic named in this lesson.
The type contract is explicit enough that another learner can explain what it accepts and rejects.
The learner records a failure case and distinguishes compile-time checks from runtime validation.
hints: Start with the syllabus item “Relating input and output types” and define the smallest example that demonstrates it.
Ask which part is checked by TypeScript and which part depends on runtime data, the environment or a test.
For external input, start with unknown and validate the required shape before using a domain type.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a successful type check as a runtime guarantee.
common_mistakes.why: Type annotations do not generally validate data after JavaScript starts running.
common_mistakes.fix: Add runtime checks for external input and tests for meaningful failure cases.

common_mistakes.problem: Using any or an assertion to silence a useful diagnostic.
common_mistakes.why: That can hide the exact mismatch the type system would otherwise report.
common_mistakes.fix: Prefer a more precise type or unknown plus narrowing; use assertions only when a verified invariant justifies them.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a compiler setting or runtime example without checking the project environment.
common_mistakes.why: Module resolution, DOM/Node globals, JSX and tool behavior depend on the configured versions and environment.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin the toolchain, match tsconfig to the runtime/bundler, and run the actual project's typecheck and tests.

summary: Generic Relationships and Constraints is taught through the subtopics listed in the source syllabus: Relating input and output types, Generic callbacks, Constraints that preserve useful information.
Prefer precise contracts and use compiler diagnostics as evidence, not as a replacement for runtime tests.
Validate untrusted data and describe environment/version assumptions explicitly.
